analysis.one_liner: Applies standard child labor rules to farm work and bans street peddling by kids under 16.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee in September 2000 and died there without a hearing or a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Children working on farms can legally do jobs at ages that would be illegal in any other industry, and can do dangerous farm jobs at 16. The CARE Act would have ended those special exemptions: farm kids would be covered by the same age rules as other child workers, the minimum age for hazardous farm work would rise from 16 to 18, kids under 16 would be barred from door-to-door and street peddling, and fines for violations would go up. It kept an exemption for kids working on their own parents' farms. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who work in agriculture — most of them the children of migrant and low-wage farmworkers — would gain protection from injuries, long hours, and hazardous machinery, since farm work currently allows them to do at younger ages what other industries cannot. All children would gain from higher fines and new criminal penalties for employers who willfully violate child labor rules in ways that kill or permanently injure a child.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the same age restrictions to agricultural employment that already apply to every other kind of work, ending the double standard in federal child labor law [S2].
Raises the minimum age for hazardous agricultural work from 16 to 18, with an exception for students who complete a certified vocational agriculture training program [S2].
Prohibits employment of children under 16 in youth peddling — selling goods door-to-door or on street corners — while preserving volunteer selling for nonprofits [S2].

Increases the maximum civil penalty for child labor violations from $10,000 to $15,000 with a $500 minimum, and adds prison time of up to five years for willful or repeat violations that kill or permanently injure a child worker [S2].
Narrows the agricultural exemption so it only covers a child working outside school hours for a parent or guardian on a farm that parent owns or operates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers — farms, farm labor contractors, and agribusiness operations that hire workers under 18 — would bear the cost of meeting the same child labor standards other industries follow, losing access to very young workers and to 16- and 17-year-olds in hazardous jobs. Companies that send children peddling goods door-to-door or on street corners would lose that labor pool. Small growers would face higher fines if they violated the rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill kept an exemption for children working on their own parents' farms, but growers who rely on young hired hands — including family farms that hire neighbors' kids — would lose flexible low-cost labor and face new compliance and paperwork burdens [S2] [S3].

Raising the hazardous-work age to 18 would bar many 16- and 17-year-olds from farm jobs they can legally hold today; the bill's answer — a training-program exception for vocational agriculture students — only works if the required training programs are actually available and affordable to rural youth [S2] [S3].

The bill delegates key protections to future Labor Department rulemaking on which farm jobs count as hazardous, meaning the real strength of the safeguard would depend on regulations written later [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a group with no other defender: children doing farm work at ages and under conditions the law forbids in every other industry, sometimes with fatal results. The costs fall on agricultural employers in the form of restricted hiring and compliance, which is the same standard every other industry already meets. The main design weakness is reliance on later regulation to define hazardous farm work, and the training exception depends on programs rural teens may not be able to reach.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended three months later.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill with three Democratic cosponsors on September 25, 2000, near the end of the 106th Congress [S1] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and with the Congress ending on January 3, 2001, it died without a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers keep the exemptions that let them hire children at ages and in hazardous jobs other industries cannot, and companies using young door-to-door sellers keep that workforce. Children working on farms remain without the protections the bill would have given them.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only four Democratic senators backing the bill and no votes or recorded opposition at all; the bill died in committee before any partisan fight could appear on a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would end the exemptions that let farms hire children at younger ages and in hazardous jobs than other industries may, and raise penalties for violations. Those exemptions exist precisely to keep cheap, young labor available to growers, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the safety of the children doing the work.

industries.industry: Youth peddling and door-to-door sales companies
industries.note: The bill would prohibit employing children under 16 to sell goods at residences, businesses, and street corners, removing a labor source that relies on young children working streets and doorsteps.

industries.industry: Family farms and agricultural education programs
industries.note: The bill preserves the exemption for children working on a parent's own farm and creates a pathway for vocational agriculture students to work in hazardous jobs after completing certified training, sparing most family operations while protecting hired child workers.
